W1001: Systematic literature reviews in software engineering require reviewers to read thousands of titles and abstracts before any full text is examined. This screening phase is slow, repetitive and expensive, and fatigue increases the risk of discarding relevant primary studies. In this paper we study whether large language models can act as title and abstract screeners. We do not try to replace reviewers. Our objective is to measure how many relevant studies a model retrieves, how much reading effort it saves, and which decisions still need a person. The contributions are a replication protocol for four published reviews, a comparison of zero-shot and few-shot prompting, and recommendations for keeping humans in control of the selection.

We replicated four software engineering reviews totalling 2,418 candidate records. For each record the model received the title, the abstract and the eligibility criteria of the original review, and answered include or exclude with a short justification. Two configurations were compared: zero-shot prompts containing only the criteria, and few-shot prompts adding six labelled examples. The decisions of the original reviewers served as the reference standard. We report recall, the proportion of relevant studies that the model keeps, precision, the proportion of kept studies that are relevant, and work saved over sampling at 95 percent recall, noted WSS@95, which estimates the reading effort avoided compared with random screening.

With few-shot prompts, the best LLM screening configuration reached a recall of 0.95 and a precision of 0.41 across the four reviews: the language model kept 95 percent of the relevant studies selected by the human reviewers. Zero-shot prompts were less reliable, as recall dropped to 0.88 and varied strongly from one review to another. Screening with the few-shot configuration reduced the number of abstracts that reviewers had to read by 52 percent, which corresponds to a WSS@95 of 0.47. Relevant studies missed by the model were mostly short abstracts with unusual vocabulary.

Human oversight remained necessary in every configuration. The model produced confident but wrong justifications for 3 percent of the records, and its explanations sometimes cited criteria that the review did not contain. We therefore recommend that the model never excludes a study on its own: every exclusion with low confidence and every disagreement between the model and a reviewer must be escalated to a human. In our protocol the final inclusion decision always belongs to the review team, and the model acts as an additional screener whose suggestions are audited.

Related work. Large language models have been proposed for many stages of systematic reviews, from query formulation to data extraction. Several position papers discuss LLM screening and generative AI assistants for study selection, in medicine and in software engineering. Most of them describe prototypes and do not report any quantitative evaluation of the screening decisions.
s2-7f3a: Prompt design strongly influences the behaviour of language models. For systematic review automation, the question is not only whether a model can classify abstracts, but which prompting strategy makes it identify the relevant studies without overwhelming reviewers with false positives. This paper compares four prompting strategies on the title and abstract stage of five reviews and reports their effect on sensitivity, specificity and cost.

We compared standard input-output prompting, zero-shot chain of thought, few-shot chain of thought with three worked examples, and majority voting over five sampled answers. All strategies used the same model, the same eligibility criteria and the same 1,850 records drawn from five published reviews. Each prompt asked the model to reason about every criterion before giving a final answer, except the input-output baseline, which returned the decision directly.

Sensitivity, the proportion of relevant studies kept by the language model during title and abstract screening, was 0.82 with input-output prompting, 0.97 with zero-shot chain of thought, and 1.00 with few-shot chain of thought and with majority voting. The gain in sensitivity came at a price: specificity decreased from 0.78 to 0.61, so reviewers received more irrelevant abstracts to check. Majority voting multiplied the cost by five, reaching 4.10 dollars per 1,000 abstracts, while few-shot chain of thought cost 0.95 dollars per 1,000 abstracts.

We adopted a human-in-the-loop workflow. The model acted as a second reviewer: two people audited all exclusions proposed by the model, and every disagreement was settled by discussion between them. No study was discarded solely on the basis of a model output. Reviewers also reported that reading the reasoning of the model helped them detect ambiguous eligibility criteria, which they clarified before the next review.

Limitations. Results depend on the wording of the prompts, and small changes produced different decisions for borderline abstracts. Hosted models are updated without notice, which threatens reproducibility; we therefore archived prompts, model versions and raw outputs. Finally, the five reviews were published before the training cut-off of the model, so data leakage cannot be excluded.
